name: Prophy paste polish

lead: Prophy paste is an abrasive polishing paste applied by a dental professional with a rotating rubber cup during a cleaning. It removes surface stain and plaque, leaving teeth looking cleaner and smoother.

Fine abrasive particles in the paste are spun against the tooth to polish the surface and lift deposits. It works on external stain rather than the tooth's inner colour. Available research is mostly laboratory work on restorative materials, porcelain and implant surfaces; no cosmetic trial of stain removal was found.

paras: It is part of a professional dental cleaning appointment, applied by a hygienist or dentist.
Lab studies show polishing pastes can change the roughness and gloss of composite resin restorations. It is a professional procedure.

angle.text: A gritty paste polishes the enamel and lifts surface stain, so teeth look cleaner and brighter right after a cleaning. Research on it focuses on abrasivity and dental materials rather than cosmetic results.

lead: Prophy paste is a gritty polishing paste applied with a rotating rubber cup, usually by a dental professional during a cleaning, to polish tooth surfaces and remove some surface deposits.[1][2] It is relevant to appearance because it is used on extrinsic (surface) stain.
The available research examines the paste mostly in the laboratory, for its effects on restorative materials, porcelain and implant surfaces, rather than as a cosmetic whitening treatment in people.

For appearance, the payoff is a cleaner, brighter-looking smile: coffee, tea, tobacco and similar causes leave extrinsic stain on the enamel surface, and a rotating rubber cup with abrasive paste is a standard way dental professionals lift it as the last step of a cleaning.[3] Wikipedia notes that extrinsic stains can often be removed mechanically, while intrinsic stains inside the tooth generally respond to whitening agents instead.[3]

paras: Dental researchers have described rubber-cup prophylaxis with pastes alongside other cleaning instruments, and one study compared prophy paste with ultrasonic and hand instruments on implant abutments.[2] Pastes have also been tested for cleaning cut dentine, where flour of pumice or a prophylaxis paste with a rubber cup was effective at removing the smear layer.[4] A review of mechanical plaque control places professional care as a supplement to daily self-care.[1]

In prophylaxis, a dental professional uses a slow-speed handpiece fitted with a rubber cup and an abrasive prophy paste, usually containing fluoride, to remove extrinsic stain; Wikipedia says each prophylaxis removes roughly one micron of enamel.[3] Before whitening, the clinician typically cleans the teeth with an ultrasonic scaler, hand instruments and possibly prophy paste to remove plaque and calculus and provide a clean surface.[3]

Polishing is also used to apply medicaments such as desensitising agents, and routine polishing has remained common in practice even though the idea of selective polishing, polishing only where stain is present, was introduced in the 1980s.[5] Manufacturers' instructions for resin sealants recommend cleaning the tooth before etching, and a 2009 review found that handpiece prophylaxis and toothbrush cleaning gave similar sealant retention in the trials examined.[6]

A 1984 randomised split-mouth trial compared the Prophy-Jet air-powder device with a rubber cup and prophylaxis paste and found the device removed plaque and stain as well in less time, with some immediate soft-tissue trauma after both methods that did not differ significantly within six days.[7] A 2013 review of air polishing notes that the traditional rubber cup with paste has been reported to remove the fluoride-rich outer layer of enamel and cause measurable loss of cementum and dentine over time, and describes air polishing as a contemporary alternative.[5]

A 2026 systematic review of professional mechanical plaque removal for gingivitis reported that split-mouth trials consistently showed ultrasonic scaling plus air polishing to be as effective as, and quicker than, ultrasonic scaling plus rubber cup with paste, though the certainty of the evidence was very low.[8] A 2021 randomised trial examined the plaque-removing efficacy of a low-abrasive air-polishing system.[9]

Laboratory work has looked at how polishing pastes affect fillings and crowns. Studies have tested surface roughness of resin composite after prophylactic pastes and toothbrushing, discoloration and gloss of a CAD/CAM resin composite after nine pastes, roughness of glass ionomer cements under five prophylaxis regimens, and roughness of dental porcelain after different polishing techniques.[10][11][12][13]

No studies found testing prophy paste as a cosmetic stain-removal or whitening treatment in people. Related work: a clinical study compared sealant retention after two tooth-cleaning techniques, and another compared prophylaxis with toothbrushing before fluoride application.[14][15] A trial examined desensitising agents on dentine hypersensitivity.[16] Laboratory studies tested how polishing pastes change roughness and gloss of composite resin and CAD/CAM composite and how polishing affects dental porcelain.[10][11][12]

The 1984 Prophy-Jet trial and the 2026 meta-analysis compare rubber-cup polishing with air polishing for plaque and stain removal, and the 2009 sealant review looks at handpiece prophylaxis as a pre-treatment step.[8][7][6]
Laboratory findings indicate that polishing pastes can change the surface roughness of resin composite materials, which is why their effect on restorations has been studied.[10][11]

timeline.event: Randomised split-mouth trial compares the Prophy-Jet with rubber cup and paste for stain and plaque removal.[7]
Review of air polishing as an alternative to rubber-cup polishing published.[5]
